newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Hartford's "Mayor Mike" leads civic rebound.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hartford's "Mayor Mike" leads civic rebound.

text.p: Steering a 1995 Buick LeSabre through the working-class neighborhoods of Hartford, Mayor Mike Peters waves regally to pedestrians, lights up another Marlboro, and is startled to discover his mustachioed face on a giant billboard.
"Holy (cow), I look like Saddam Hussein," he tells a passenger, then resumes his narrative on the underrated virtues of Connecticut's capital city.
The feisty, blue-collar "Mayor Mike," as he is generally known, functions as chief morale officer and comedian at large in a city that has not had much to laugh about in recent years.
Like many U.S. cities, Hartford is trying with scant public funds to fight rapid population loss, corporate downsizing, rising social service needs and a crumbled manufacturing base.

To add insult to injury, the city recently suffered the loss of Connecticut's only major league sports team -- the National Hockey League's Hartford Whalers -- and saw its beleagured public school system taken over by the state.

Although it's not in his nature to sulk, hockey fan Mayor Mike took the Whalers loss hard. The day after the team announced it was leaving, Peters told reporters he felt like slapping team owner Peter Karmanos in the back of the head.
Peters and other civic leaders are now figuring out how to replace the $73 million pumped into Hartford's economy each year by the Whalers, who had been in town since 1975.

Hartford's population has shrunk from 180,000 in the 1950s to 126,000 today. Blacks, whites and Hispanics each make up roughly one third of the population, although black and Hispanic children represent a whopping 94 percent of enrollment in the troubled school system.
SIMMERING BOUILLABAISSE
The once-proud insurance capital has been reduced to "a simmering bouillabaisse of urban pathologies," columnist George F. Will wrote last year.
Connecticut has lost 10,000 to 12,000 insurance jobs in the last six years, mostly in Hartford, according to the state department of labor. Hartford insurance employment is now around 46,000.
And yet many Hartford residents and suburbanites feel the city is clawing its way back from its darkest days, thanks largely to Democrat Peters, 48.

The past two years have seen dramatic reductions in violent crime. Gang murders among Latino youth have been virtually eliminated, after Peters successfully lobbied for increased federal funds for community policing. Small businesses and even some big corporations, such as distiller Heublein Inc., have moved back downtown.

The city's notorious Charter Oak Terrace housing project is being torn down and redeveloped, and the Connecticut River area is undergoing a $35 million restoration as an important economic and recreational resource for the city.

Remarkably, Peters has led the revival with little in the way of formal political power. Policy is set by the city council, on which he doesn't have a vote, while government departments are run by a city manager.
"To me, the fascinating thing is that this mayor does not have the kind administrative power that most mayors do have," said Susan Coes, manager of the Metro Hartford News Bureau.
PERSONALITY NOT POWER
"He has done it all by force of personality, rather than by legislative or administrative fiat," she added.
Coes said Peters -- who was re-elected in 1995 with 88 percent of the vote -- is greeted like a beloved celebrity whenever he walks the streets of Hartford or the suburbs.

The energetic Peters is about as far removed from the slick, professional politician as it's possible to get. A native of the city's Italian South End (his grandfather changed the family name from Pierantonio), Peters was a firefighter for 22 years before deciding to run for mayor in 1993.
"When I told my family I was running for mayor, they laughed for 20 minutes," Peters told Reuters.
Driving around the city with a reporter, Peters frequently interrupts his travelogue with the aside, "I once put out a fire in that house."
A cruise past staid old Trinity College prompts the remark, "I answered so many false alarms at Trinity, I should have picked up a degree while I was there."
A life-long working stiff, Peters did not attend college.

"We've taken some tough blows with losing some major companies and losing local ownership and the influence of local CEOs," said Ed Morgan, president of the Hartford Downtown Council. "But Mike has been able to galvanize the others, and I don't think he lets people get down."
